name: Evergreen Collaborative (Giving Green, 2021)
beneficiaries_note: Climate: the good of a tonne of CO₂ averted is spread over the world, by population.
summary: US climate policy. A re-implementation of Giving Green's 2021 estimate of what Evergreen's advocacy for a Clean Electricity Performance Program (CEPP) and the Clean Energy for America Act (CEAA) tax credits cost per tonne of CO₂e avoided. Superseded by Giving Green's 2022 estimate, which counts on the rankings.

sections.title: Power sector emissions under business as usual and the bills
From cost per tonne to tonnes per dollar
sections.explainer: charityevals' step after Giving Green's bottom line: Giving Green reports dollars per tonne; the site needs tonnes per dollar, and how much air pollution those tonnes cut. The cuts come mostly from US power plants burning less coal and gas, which emit a small fraction of the world-average smoke per tonne (docs/normalization.md 2.5). The tonnes come years after the money is spent, so they are discounted for that wait at the site's discount rate.

sections.title: Staff pay below market
sections.explainer: charityevals' step, not Giving Green's: with credit by share of resources on, staff's pay below what they could earn elsewhere counts as an in-kind contribution and gets its share of the outcome. Off by default.

rows.label: Evergreen's spending on clean energy tax credits
rows.explainer: What Evergreen spent on the clean energy tax credits (the CEAA), from its 501(c)(3) and 501(c)(4), as Giving Green records it.

rows.label: Evergreen Action's 501(c)(4) spending on the CEPP
rows.explainer: Television advertising for the Clean Electricity Performance Program.

rows.label: Evergreen Collaborative's 501(c)(3) spending on the CEPP
rows.explainer: Modelling, staff and consulting time and digital work on the CEPP.

rows.label: Evergreen's total spending on these bills
Reduction in power sector emissions 2022–30 with the CEPP (million tonnes)
rows.explainer: From the sheet's 'CEPP and CEAA' tab: the extra cut in US power-sector emissions from 2022 to 2030 with the CEPP on top of the tax credits, from Resources for the Future's projections of power-sector emissions under the CEAA alone and under the CEAA with the CEPP.

rows.label: Reduction in power sector emissions 2022–30 with the CEAA (million tonnes)
rows.explainer: From the sheet's 'CEPP and CEAA' tab: the cut in US power-sector emissions from 2022 to 2030 with the Clean Energy for America Act's tax credits.

rows.label: Change in probability of a bill passing with the CEPP due to Evergreen
rows.explainer: Giving Green's pessimistic, realistic and optimistic cases: 0.5%, 1% and 3%, kept low because Evergreen was one of many organisations pushing the CEPP. Low and high are Giving Green's pessimistic and optimistic scenarios, not a confidence interval.

rows.label: Change in probability of a bill passing with the CEAA due to Evergreen
rows.explainer: Giving Green takes a tenth of Evergreen's effect on the CEPP (0.05%, 0.1% and 0.3%): many organisations pushed for the tax credits, and the CEPP was Evergreen's higher priority.

rows.label: Expected value of Evergreen in changing CO₂e emissions (million tonnes)
Cost per tonne of CO₂e
rows.explainer: Giving Green's 2021 bottom line, realistic case: about $0.54 a tonne ($1.08 pessimistic, $0.18 optimistic). In 2022 Giving Green judged it no longer relevant, because the CEPP was left out of the Inflation Reduction Act, and replaced it with an estimate for Evergreen's work on implementing the Inflation Reduction Act.

rows.label: Change in CO₂e per dollar (tonnes per $)
Years from the grant until the tonnes are avoided
rows.explainer: Giving Green counts Evergreen's 2021 spending against the cuts in US power-sector emissions from 2022 to 2030, which grow over the period as clean power is built, so the average tonne comes about six years after the money is spent. Our judgment from Giving Green's dates. Giving Green counts a tonne the same whenever it is avoided; the site discounts every future benefit at the discount rate under Your values, in both views (an evaluator stating dollars per tonne takes no view on discounting). The heat deaths a tonne avoids are discounted again from the year it is avoided, in the site's climate conversion.

rows.label: How much the next dollar does compared with the average dollar so far
rows.explainer: Your value, one figure for every model built on an organisation's past average (Your values: "How much the next dollar does compared with the average dollar so far"): the cost per tonne is Evergreen's past spending on two bills over their expected effect, an average; the next dollar does less than the average dollar did, since an organisation pursues its best opportunities first. 50% by default (our judgment), from 18% to 100% (average = marginal). The evaluator view keeps 100%.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted per dollar
rows.explainer: One over Giving Green's cost per tonne, discounted for the wait until the tonnes are avoided, like every future benefit on the site. How much air pollution these tonnes cut is the rows below. A marginal dollar is counted at the share of the past average you set (row above).

rows.label: Share of these tonnes from burning less fuel
rows.explainer: Most of the CEPP's and CEAA's cuts come from US power plants burning less coal and gas. Set to 1 because the health studies in the next row count deaths avoided per tonne of the whole package, so the tonnes that don't come from burning less fuel are already averaged into that figure.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne cut by US clean-electricity policy, relative to the fossil-fuel average

source.title: Energy Innovation (2022) and Resources for the Future (2022), health modelling of the Inflation Reduction Act
source.note: Deaths avoided in 2030: about 3,700–3,900 (Energy Innovation), 700–1,300 (Resources for the Future), from roughly a billion tonnes cut that year.

rows.explainer: Per fuel and place, not the world average: US power plants mostly have scrubbers. Health modelling of the Inflation Reduction Act projects about 3,700–3,900 deaths avoided in 2030 (Energy Innovation, 2022) or 700–1,300 (Resources for the Future, 2022), from roughly a billion tonnes cut that year: 0.7 to 3.9 deaths per million tonnes, 0.005 to 0.027 of the world average of 1.46 per 10,000. Best guess 0.013, the middle of the two studies' central figures on a log scale.

rows.label: Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: The row the site's climate conversion reads (docs/normalization.md 2.5): the air-pollution deaths each of these tonnes avoids, as a multiple of the world average behind the shared rate, 1.46 air-pollution deaths per 10,000 tonnes of CO₂ from fossil fuels (Rethink Priorities). The conversion values every tonne for its heat deaths (discounted over the decades until they come) and adds "Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂"'s air-pollution part times this row, at once. Here: the US health studies' deaths per tonne, relative to the world average.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths averted per tonne, counted directly by the evaluator (none here)
rows.explainer: A row every climate model has, which the site's conversion reads (docs/normalization.md 2.5): air-pollution deaths the evaluator counts itself, per tonne, on top of what the tonnes carry through air_pollution_weight. The evaluator counts none for this charity, so 0.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of program cost
rows.explainer: Default for research, technical assistance and policy work: mostly people. Our judgment; we haven't seen this charity's breakdown. Evergreen's CEPP spending included $0.5 million of television advertising, so the true share may be lower.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: Policy staff and former government officials could typically earn considerably more in law firms, consulting or lobbying. Our judgment.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff per dollar of cost (in-kind donation)
Share of the full cost paid in cash
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, staff's forgone pay counts as part of the cost, and staff get their share of the outcome. Off, this is 100%.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted per dollar donated
rows.explainer: The tonnes per dollar above; with credit by share of resources, times the share of the full cost paid in cash (staff's forgone pay is the rest). The site turns these tonnes into years of healthy life through the deaths they avoid: "Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂", its heat part discounted over "Years until the heat deaths from a tonne of CO₂" for every tonne, and its air-pollution part, at once, times "Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne" above.
